summary.text: Hubble's law, officially the Hubble–Lemaître law, is the observation that galaxies are moving away from Earth at speeds proportional to their distance.
So the farther a galaxy is from Earth, the faster it moves away, and its speed is typically found by measuring its redshift.
It is considered the first observational basis for the expansion of the universe and is one of the pieces of evidence most often cited for the Big Bang model.

facts.label: Equation
facts.value: v = H₀D: speed is H₀ times distance

facts.label: Example speed
facts.value: A galaxy 1 megaparsec (3.09×10¹⁹ km) away recedes at 70 km/s

facts.label: Growth rate
facts.value: H₀ = 7%/Gyr: structures grow 7% per billion years

facts.label: Published by Hubble
facts.value: Edwin Hubble published his work in 1929

items.prompt: Galaxy A is three times as far from us as galaxy B. How do their speeds of moving away compare?

options.label: A moves away at the same speed as B
A moves away three times as fast as B
B moves away three times as fast as A
A moves away nine times as fast as B

items.explain: Speed is proportional to distance, so three times the distance means three times the speed.

items.prompt: In Hubble's law, a galaxy's speed and its distance are both worked out indirectly. How?

options.label: Speed comes from its redshift and distance from its brightness
Speed comes from its brightness and distance from its redshift
Both come from timing radio signals sent to the galaxy
Both come from weighing the galaxy's total mass

items.explain: The velocities and distances in the law are not directly measured: velocity is inferred from redshift and distance from brightness.

items.prompt: A scientist plots speed against distance for many galaxies. What shape shows Hubble's law?

options.label: A curve that levels off at large distance
A cluster of dots with no pattern
A straight line that slopes upward
A straight line that slopes downward

items.explain: On a Hubble diagram a straight line of positive slope depicts the law.

items.prompt: Why do many people now credit Lemaître alongside Hubble?

options.label: He built the telescope that Hubble used
He showed that Hubble's results were mistaken
He measured the redshifts that Hubble's data used
He published the same relationship two years before Hubble did

items.explain: Lemaître in 1927 was the first to publish research deriving what is now known as Hubble's law, two years before Hubble.

items.prompt: The Hubble constant is the present value of a quantity that changes. What does that quantity do?

options.label: The Hubble parameter varies with time
The Hubble parameter keeps one value forever
The Hubble parameter measures only nearby stars
The Hubble parameter falls to zero at every instant

items.explain: The Hubble constant is constant at any given moment, but the Hubble parameter of which it is the current value varies with time.

items.prompt: What was Einstein's cosmological constant originally inserted to achieve?

options.label: A faster expansion, so galaxies would fly apart
A static solution, so the universe would not change
A way to measure redshift, so distances were fixed
A shrinking universe, so stars would be pulled in

items.explain: Einstein put the term into his equations to coerce them into the static solution; he abandoned it after Hubble's discovery was published.

paragraphs.heading: Farther means faster
paragraphs.text: Hubble's law, officially called the Hubble–Lemaître law, says that galaxies are moving away from Earth at speeds in proportion to how far away they are. Double the distance and you double the speed. It is seen as the first observational foundation for the expanding universe, and it is among the most cited pieces of evidence for the Big Bang model.

paragraphs.heading: Reading speed and distance
paragraphs.text: Neither the speed nor the distance in Hubble's law is measured directly. The speed comes from redshift, a shift in the frequency of the light a galaxy sends out, written z = ∆λ/λ. The distance comes from how bright the galaxy appears. Plot speed against distance on a Hubble diagram, and the law shows up as a straight line sloping upward.

paragraphs.heading: The Hubble constant
paragraphs.text: The law is written v = H₀D, where v is how fast a galaxy is separating from us, D is its distance, and H₀ is the Hubble constant. Its units are km/s/Mpc, which means a galaxy 1 megaparsec (3.09×10¹⁹ km) away recedes at 70 km/s. Put another way, H₀ = 7%/Gyr: at today's rate, a structure not held together by gravity grows by 7% in a billion years. The name constant is a little misleading, since the underlying Hubble parameter changes over time and H₀ is just its present value.

paragraphs.heading: Who found it first
paragraphs.text: Edwin Hubble is credited for work he published in 1929, but others got there earlier. In 1922 Alexander Friedmann derived from general relativity that the universe might be expanding at a rate that could be calculated. Carl Wilhelm Wirtz, in 1922 and 1924, found that smaller, dimmer galaxies had larger redshifts. In 1927 Georges Lemaître noticed that distant objects recede at speeds in step with their distances and estimated the ratio, which later became known as the Hubble constant.

paragraphs.heading: Hubble's own path
paragraphs.text: Hubble did most of his observing at Mount Wilson Observatory, which then had the most powerful telescope in the world. By studying Cepheid variable stars in the so-called spiral nebulae, he worked out their distances and found them to lie far outside the Milky Way. He combined his distances with redshifts measured by Vesto Slipher and Milton Humason and found a rough proportion between redshift and distance.

paragraphs.heading: Einstein changes course
paragraphs.text: Before this, Einstein had added a term called the cosmological constant to his equations of general relativity to force them to describe a static universe, which he then believed was correct. Once Hubble's discovery was published, Einstein dropped his work on that term. Hubble's observations also settled an older argument: in the 1920 Shapley–Curtis debate, Shapley held that the universe was the size of the Milky Way, while Curtis argued it was much bigger. His improved observations in the following decade resolved the question.
